cards.title: Conditionally remove jQuery for logged-out front-end visitors
cards.claim: In this WordPress example, jQuery was needed for logged-in users because of the admin bar, but was removed for logged-out front-end visitors with a code snippet.
cards.action: Configure the snippet to run only on the front end and only when the user is not logged in; dequeue and deregister jQuery under those conditions.
applies_when: jQuery is loading for logged-out visitors
Logged-in users still need jQuery for the WordPress admin bar
do_not_use_when: The request is not on the front end
Removing jQuery would break required front-end functionality
unknowns: Which exact code snippet/filter implementation was used
Whether theme or plugin scripts require jQuery for logged-out visitors
evidence_quotes: "It's necessary for loggedin users because the WordPress admin bar uses jQuery"
"there's absolutely no reason that a logged out user should be loading jQuery when they visit our site."
"I'm telling the snippet only to run if it's on the front end."
"make sure it only runs if the user is not logged in."
"we need to dq and dregister jQuery"

cards.title: Unload WooCommerce assets only on a page that does not need them
cards.claim: The example uses Asset CleanUp to disable WooCommerce files on a landing page while retaining assets that may still be needed elsewhere.
cards.action: On the specific landing page, use Asset CleanUp to unload WooCommerce assets that the page does not need; retain or revisit assets if WooCommerce features are later added.
applies_when: A specific landing page currently does not use WooCommerce features
WooCommerce assets are loading on that page
do_not_use_when: The page needs WooCommerce functionality such as a mini cart
You have not verified which WooCommerce files the page requires
unknowns: Which listed WooCommerce files are safe to unload on other sites
Whether the WooCommerce coming-soon CSS file is required
evidence_quotes: "we also had a bunch of Woo Commerce stuff loading which we don't need on the landing page in its current state."
"the easiest way to unload stuff like that on specific pages is a plugin called asset cleanup."
"We might in the future. So, remember that you've unloaded this if you ever decide to add Woo Commerce features [music] to the landing page, like a mini cart, for instance."
"that's going to unload it just on this page"
"Asset cleanup lets you kind of surgically remove things on specific pages while keeping stuff active where it needs to be."

cards.title: Verify compression and cache status in response headers
cards.claim: The example checks the first network request's response headers to confirm gzip compression and a cache hit after enabling server caching and compression.
cards.action: In browser dev tools, inspect the first network request's response headers; look for a content-encoding value such as gzip and a cache-related hit header after enabling the relevant server settings.
applies_when: Compression and caching have been enabled or need verification
You can inspect browser network response headers
do_not_use_when: Interpreting "cache-control" alone as proof of a cache hit
unknowns: Which cache header and encoding method a particular host uses
Whether a cache hit will use an "x-cache" header on every server
evidence_quotes: "If you have caching enabled, you'll see something related to caching. Not cache control cuz this is saying no cache must revalidate, but you should see something like Xcache or something that says hit related to caching."
"You should also see content encoding and it should mention gzip or whatever your encoding method is here in the response headers."
"content encoding gzip, which tells us we have compression enabled."
"we have this x-cache response header that says hit. That means it's hitting the cache."
